title: The Pazyryk Carpet
about: This is the oldest knotted-pile carpet known. It was found in 1949 in a frozen burial mound, where ice had kept it intact for more than two thousand years. The center is a grid of star-like flowers. Around it run borders of grazing deer and a slow parade of riders, some on horseback and some walking beside their horses. For people whose lives depended on horses, it reads as a picture of what mattered: animals, order and wealth carried with you.
artistBio: The weavers are unknown. They belonged to, or traded with, the Pazyryk people, nomadic horse herders related to the Scythians who buried their leaders with horses, clothing and textiles. Some scholars think the carpet was made in Persia or Armenia and carried north. Either way, it shows that the hand-knotting technique behind later Persian and Turkish rugs was already mature by this time. It is now in the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.

title: The Paracas Textile
medium: Cotton and camelid fiber, cross-knit looping
about: A cotton mantle bordered with dozens of tiny three-dimensional figures, each only a few inches tall. They hold fans, staffs, plants and severed heads, and wear masks and headdresses. Each figure is different. Scholars read them as people in ritual dress, possibly ancestors or shamans in transformation. The textile was most likely made to wrap the dead, and it carried meaning about power, fertility and the passage between worlds.
artistBio: The Paracas people lived on Peru's dry southern coast about two thousand years ago. Their large burial grounds held mummy bundles wrapped in hundreds of fine textiles, preserved by the desert. The makers worked with a needle in a looping technique so fine it looks knitted. Their names are lost, but their work set the standard for Andean textiles that followed. This piece is at the Brooklyn Museum.

title: The Hestia Tapestry
about: The Greek goddess of the hearth sits on a throne, covered in jewels. A Greek inscription names her "Hestia full of blessings." Six small boys bring her discs, each labeled with a gift: wealth, joy, praise, abundance, virtue and progress. It was likely a wall hanging for a home, wishing good fortune on the household, made at a time when Egypt was Christian but still used old pagan images as signs of plenty.
artistBio: The weavers worked in Egypt during the Byzantine period, when tapestry weaving in wool and linen was a major industry. Many such textiles survive because Egypt's dry ground preserved them in burials. The makers are unnamed. Their skill shows in the shading, done by blending colored threads the way a painter blends paint. The tapestry is at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington, D.C.

title: The Bayeux Tapestry
about: Despite its name, this is embroidery, not tapestry. It is about 70 meters long and half a meter tall, and it tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066. It shows Harold's oath to William, Halley's comet, the building of ships, and the Battle of Hastings. It is the Norman version of events: Harold breaks his oath, and William's victory looks deserved. It works like a comic strip and like political argument at the same time.
artistBio: It was most likely commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror's half-brother, and stitched in England, probably in Canterbury. English needlework was famous across Europe, and the work was likely done by teams of skilled embroiderers, many of them women. Their names were never recorded. The piece has hung in Bayeux, in Normandy, for most of its life.

title: The Överhogdal Tapestries
about: Long bands crowded with horses, elk, dogs, ships, buildings and riders. They were found in the early 1900s in a church storeroom in the small village of Överhogdal. Their meaning is still debated. Some see scenes of Ragnarök, the Norse end of the world. Others point to Christian symbols, such as churches and what may be the Star of Bethlehem. They likely come from the time when the region was moving from the old gods to Christianity, and they may hold both.
artistBio: The makers are unknown, probably women in a farming community in northern Sweden. Radiocarbon dating places the textiles roughly between the 900s and the 1100s. They are among the very few Viking-age figure textiles to survive. They are now kept at Jamtli, the regional museum in Östersund.

title: The Syon Cope
medium: Silk and metal thread on linen
about: A priest's cope, a large semicircular cloak worn for processions and solemn liturgies. Interlocking shapes hold scenes of Christ, the Virgin Mary and the apostles, with angels in the spaces between. It is a teaching image as well as a vestment: the whole story of salvation wraps around the wearer's body. The name comes from Syon Abbey, whose Bridgettine nuns kept it through centuries of exile after the Reformation and brought it back to England in the 1800s.
artistBio: This is opus anglicanum, "English work," the embroidery that made medieval England famous. Professional workshops in London, staffed by both men and women, produced vestments prized by popes and kings. Embroiderers used split stitch for faces and underside couching for gold, which let the heavy cloth bend without breaking. The cope is at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: The Apocalypse Tapestry
artist: Jean Bondol (design) and the workshop of Nicolas Bataille
about: The largest medieval tapestry set to survive, about 100 meters of what was once around 140. It illustrates the Book of Revelation scene by scene: the four horsemen, the seven-headed beast, the woman clothed with the sun, the new Jerusalem. It was made in the years of plague and the Hundred Years' War, when the end of the world felt close. It is also a statement of power by its patron, who could afford the most ambitious textile of its time.
artistBio: Louis I, Duke of Anjou, commissioned it. The court painter Jean Bondol, also called Hennequin of Bruges, drew the designs, working from illuminated manuscripts. The weaving was done in Paris by the workshop of Nicolas Bataille. It survived revolution and neglect and now hangs in a purpose-built gallery at the Château d'Angers.

title: The Hunt of the Unicorn
medium: Wool, silk, silver and gilt thread
about: Seven tapestries follow hunters as they track, wound and kill a unicorn, which then appears alive again, chained in a small round fence under a pomegranate tree. Medieval viewers could read it two ways at once. As religion, the unicorn is Christ, killed and risen. As love, it is the lover captured by the beloved, and the pomegranates suggest marriage and fertility. More than a hundred plants are shown so accurately that botanists can name most of them.
artistBio: The designers and weavers are unknown. The set was probably designed in Paris and woven in Brussels or a nearby center, the best tapestry workshops in Europe at the time. For centuries it belonged to the La Rochefoucauld family. John D. Rockefeller Jr. gave it to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and it hangs at The Met Cloisters in New York.

title: The Lady and the Unicorn
about: Six tapestries on a red ground scattered with flowers and small animals. Five show the senses: touch, taste, smell, hearing and sight. In the sixth, the lady stands before a tent inscribed "À mon seul désir," "to my only desire," placing a necklace into a box. The meaning is still argued. She may be giving up the pleasures of the senses for a higher love, or choosing love as the sixth sense that joins the others.
artistBio: The designs are linked to a Paris artist known as the Master of Anne of Brittany, and the weaving was done in Flanders. The banners carry the coat of arms of the Le Viste family of Lyon. The tapestries were rediscovered in a French château in the 1840s, and the novelist George Sand helped make them famous. They are at the Musée de Cluny in Paris.

title: The Ardabil Carpet
about: A huge carpet, more than ten meters long, with a golden sunburst medallion at its center, ringed by sixteen pointed shapes. Two mosque lamps of different sizes hang from it, one on each end, a clever way to fake perspective for someone standing at one end. It was made for the shrine of Sheikh Safi al-Din at Ardabil. A poem by Hafez is woven into one end, followed by the maker's humble signature, describing himself as a servant of the court.
artistBio: The inscription names Maqsud of Kashan, likely the designer or the head of the workshop rather than a single weaver. Carpets like this took teams of weavers years to finish. It is one of a pair made under the Safavid shah Tahmasp. The Victoria and Albert Museum bought it in 1893 on William Morris's advice. Its twin, cut down to repair it, is at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

title: Royal Tunic with Tocapu
about: A man's tunic covered in a grid of more than a hundred small squares called tocapu, almost none repeated. Some are versions of designs from other Inca tunics, which suggests it gathers the whole empire into one garment. It was most likely made for the ruler himself. The Inca had no written script, and some scholars think tocapu were a kind of symbolic language. In the Andes, fine cloth was worth more than gold and was given as a royal gift.
artistBio: The finest Inca cloth, called cumbi, was woven by specialists: the aqllakuna, women chosen to live and work in state compounds, and male weavers called qumpikamayuq. This tunic has a very dense thread count, near the upper limit of what hand weaving can do. The makers' names are not known. The tunic is at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington, D.C.

title: Khipu (Quipu)
about: A khipu is a bundle of knotted cords hanging from a main cord. Knot types and their positions recorded numbers in a base-ten system: census counts, tribute, stores in warehouses. Colors, twist direction and how cords attach carried more information. Some researchers think khipus also recorded names or stories. If so, this is writing done in thread, a record of an empire that could be carried on the back of a runner.
artistBio: Specialists called khipukamayuq, "keepers of the knots," made and read khipus for the Inca state. Earlier Andean cultures such as the Wari also used knotted cords. After the Spanish conquest, khipukamayuq still read their records aloud in colonial courts. Several hundred khipus survive in museums, and the work of fully decoding them is still under way.

f: Shawl from Kashmir, mid-19th century, Honolulu Museum of Art, 3976.1.JPG
title: Kashmir Shawl
about: Kashmir shawls were woven from pashm, the soft undercoat of mountain goats, using dozens of small wooden bobbins called kani to build up the pattern thread by thread. The bent teardrop motif, the boteh, became wildly popular in Europe. When mills in Paisley, Scotland, began making cheaper copies, the shape took the town's name. A shawl moved between worlds: a Mughal court gift, then a fashion item in Paris and London.
artistBio: The weavers were mostly men working in workshops in and around Srinagar. A master read the pattern from a coded script and called it out to weavers at the loom. A single fine shawl could take more than a year. Mughal emperors prized them, and later European demand reshaped the industry. Kani shawls are still made in Kashmir today.

f: 朱克柔缂丝莲塘乳鸭图.jpg
title: Kesi Silk Tapestry
about: Kesi means "carved silk." Each color stops at the edge of its shape, leaving tiny slits that look as if the design was cut out. In the Song dynasty, weavers began copying paintings in kesi: birds on branches, flowers, butterflies. The result looks painted until you are close. It shows how Chinese art did not separate painting from weaving. A silk could be read and admired just like a scroll.
artistBio: Zhu Kerou is one of the few weavers from early China known by name, and she was a woman. She worked in the Southern Song period, from Songjiang near today's Shanghai. Her kesi of ducks in a lotus pond, camellias, birds and insects were collected by the imperial court and signed with her seal. Works attributed to her are at the Liaoning Provincial Museum and the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

title: Kente Cloth
about: Kente is woven in narrow strips, a few inches wide, then sewn edge to edge into a large cloth. Each pattern has a name, often tied to a proverb, a historical event or a person. Colors carry meaning too: gold for wealth and status, green for growth, black for maturity and the ancestors. Once reserved for Asante royalty, kente is now worn at graduations and celebrations as a sign of African and diaspora identity.
artistBio: A story from the Asante town of Bonwire says two weavers learned the craft by watching Ananse the spider spin its web. Kente is traditionally woven by men on narrow horizontal looms. The Ewe people to the east have their own tradition with more pictorial motifs. Weavers still work in Bonwire, Adanwomase and Ewe towns such as Agotime.

title: Bògòlanfini (Mud Cloth)
medium: Cotton dyed with plant dye and fermented mud
about: The cloth is first soaked in a yellow dye made from leaves, which bonds with the iron-rich mud painted on afterward. The mud turns the background dark and leaves the pattern pale. Traditional patterns are abstract signs with names and stories. The cloth was worn by hunters for protection and by women after major life passages. Bògòlanfini means "mud cloth," and in Mali it is about strength and protection as much as beauty.
artistBio: Men weave the cotton strips; women dye and paint the cloth, a knowledge passed from mother to daughter. Nakunte Diarra of Kolokani became one of the best-known traditional practitioners. In the 1970s, artist collectives such as Groupe Bogolan Kasobane in Bamako brought the technique into contemporary painting and fashion.

f: Raffia cloth, Kuba kingdom, c. 1909, HMA.JPG
title: Kuba Raffia Cloth
medium: Raffia palm fiber, embroidery and cut pile
about: Square panels and long wrap skirts covered in geometric patterns that shift and break just as you think you have found the rule. Some are cut-pile, like velvet. Each pattern has a name. The long skirts were worn at important ceremonies, and they were buried with the dead, so a person entered the afterlife dressed in their family's wealth. European modernists, Matisse among them, collected these cloths and admired their freedom.
artistBio: In the Kuba kingdom, men grew the raffia palm and wove the plain panels. Women did the embroidery and cut-pile work, often improvising the design as they went. Groups such as the Shoowa became known for the finest pile cloth. Kuba weaving continues in the Kasai region today.

title: Chilkat Robe
medium: Mountain goat wool and cedar bark
about: A five-sided dancing robe with a long fringe that sways as the wearer moves. The designs are formline images of clan crests, such as the bear, raven or killer whale, broken into eyes, ovoids and curves. Chilkat is the only weaving tradition in the world that can make true circles in a twined textile. Robes are worn at ceremonies and are treated as living things that carry clan history.
artistBio: Women weave Chilkat, working from pattern boards that were traditionally painted by men. The technique likely began among the Tsimshian and was perfected by the Chilkat Tlingit. A single robe can take a year or more. Jennie Thlunaut (1892–1986) kept the art alive by teaching many weavers late in her life, and the practice is strong again today.

title: Navajo (Diné) Weaving
about: Diné weavers make blankets and rugs with bold stripes, terraced diamonds and, later, regional styles like Two Grey Hills. The Diné say Spider Woman taught them to weave, and Spider Man built the first loom. Some weavers leave a small line of contrasting thread leading out of the border, a weaver's pathway, so the spirit put into the work is not trapped. A rug is a prayer as much as a product.
artistBio: Weaving has passed mostly through women, mother to daughter. One of its best-known figures is Hosteen Klah (1867–1937), a respected healer and weaver who was nádleehi, a recognized gender role in Diné tradition. He wove sacred sandpainting designs into permanent tapestries and helped found the Wheelwright Museum in Santa Fe.

title: ʻAhu ʻula (Feather Cloak)
medium: Feathers tied to olonā fiber netting
about: A cloak of tens of thousands of red and yellow feathers tied onto a net of olonā fiber. Only high chiefs, the aliʻi, could wear them, in battle and in ceremony. The feathers came from small forest birds, and gathering enough took years. In 1779 the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu gave his cloak to Captain James Cook. It returned to Hawaiʻi in 2016, after more than two centuries away.
artistBio: Skilled makers, often men of high rank, tied each small bundle of feathers into the net, a task that could take generations for one cloak. Bird catchers collected the feathers from birds such as the ʻiʻiwi and the ʻōʻō. Several of these birds are now extinct. Hawaiian practitioners today are reviving the craft with feathers gathered ethically.

f: Mola (blouse panel), Cuna (Kuna) Indians, Honolulu Museum of Art, 3740.1.JPG
title: Mola
about: A mola is a panel made by stacking layers of colored cloth and cutting down through them, folding back the edges to reveal the colors below. Two panels form the front and back of a woman's blouse. Designs grew out of earlier body painting and now include animals, plants, myths and modern life. In 1925 the Guna rose up against Panamanian officials who tried to ban their dress, and the mola remains a symbol of Guna self-rule.
artistBio: Molas are made by Guna women, who learn as girls and often work on several at once. A fine mola can take weeks. Each woman develops her own style, and molas are traded, gifted and sold. The tradition supports families in Guna Yala and in Panama City.

title: Chilean Arpilleras
artist: Women of Santiago's shantytowns; Violeta Parra
about: Small scenes stitched from scraps of clothing: the Andes, a sun, a row of houses, and women holding photographs and asking where their family members are. Under Pinochet's dictatorship, these cloths told what newspapers could not, about the disappeared, hunger and protest. The Catholic Church's Vicariate of Solidarity in Santiago bought them and sent them abroad, so the women earned money and the world heard their story.
artistBio: The folk singer Violeta Parra made arpilleras in the 1960s and showed them at the Louvre's decorative arts museum in 1964. After 1973, workshops of mothers, wives and sisters of the disappeared took the form in a new direction. Their names often went unrecorded for their safety. Their work inspired similar movements in Peru, Northern Ireland and elsewhere.

title: Hmong Story Cloth
place: Refugee camps in Thailand; later the U.S.
about: Rows of tiny embroidered figures: villages, soldiers, people fleeing through the jungle, crossing the Mekong River at night, arriving in camps. Older Hmong needlework, called paj ntaub or "flower cloth," was mostly geometric. After the war in Laos, Hmong people began stitching their story in pictures. The cloths hold memory for a community whose language had only recently been written down.
artistBio: Story cloths began in refugee camps such as Ban Vinai in Thailand. Often men drew the designs and women did the stitching, and the cloths were sold to support families. Many makers later resettled in the United States, France and Australia, where the tradition continues and now also tells stories of new lives.

title: Nakshi Kantha
medium: Running stitch on layered old saris
about: Old saris and cloths are layered and stitched together with a simple running stitch, then embroidered with lotus flowers, fish, wheels, people and animals. Nothing is wasted: worn cloth becomes a quilt, a wrap or a cover for a newborn. The poet Jasimuddin's 1929 poem "The Field of the Embroidered Quilt" tells of a young widow who stitches her grief into a kantha. These cloths often carry a family's life story.
artistBio: Kantha is made by women at home, often over months, using threads drawn from the colored borders of old saris. Each family has its own motifs. In the 20th century, groups in Bangladesh and India revived nakshi kantha as a source of income for rural women, and it is now a recognized art form.

title: Phulkari Bagh
medium: Untwisted silk floss on handspun cotton
about: Phulkari means "flower work." Women stitch from the back of the cloth with untwisted silk, mostly gold and orange, in a darning stitch that catches the light. When the stitching covers the whole cloth, it is called a bagh, a garden. A grandmother might begin a bagh when a girl was born, to be given at her wedding. It carries love and blessing from one generation of women to the next.
artistBio: The makers were women in Punjabi villages, Hindu, Sikh and Muslim, working without a drawn pattern and counting the threads of the cloth. The partition of 1947 disrupted the tradition. Today, cooperatives and designers are bringing phulkari back.

title: Uzbek Ikat (Abr)
place: Bukhara, Samarkand and the Fergana Valley
about: In ikat, the threads are tied and dyed before they are woven, so the pattern appears as the cloth is made, with soft, blurred edges. In Uzbek it is called abr, "cloud," for that misty look. Bold robes in these silks were worn and given as signs of wealth and honor. The pattern is not printed on the surface but built into the thread itself.
artistBio: Making abr took a chain of specialists: pattern-binders, dyers for each color and weavers. In Bukhara, Jewish dyers were known for their indigo work. Soviet industry nearly ended the craft, but workshops in Margilan and elsewhere revived it after 1991.

title: Javanese Batik
about: Hot wax is drawn onto cloth with a small copper tool called a canting. Where the wax sits, dye cannot reach. The cloth is waxed and dyed again and again to build up colors. Each motif has meaning, and some, like the diagonal parang pattern, were once reserved for the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta. Batik marks births, weddings and deaths in Java. UNESCO recognized it in 2009.
artistBio: Hand-drawn batik, called batik tulis, has mostly been made by women, while stamped batik using copper blocks is often men's work. Coastal towns like Pekalongan mixed Chinese, Dutch and Arab influences into their designs, while court batik kept older, quieter colors. Indonesia celebrates National Batik Day each October 2.

title: Boro
medium: Patched and stitched indigo cotton and hemp
about: Boro means "rags." These are jackets and bedcovers patched over and over, layer upon layer, held with running stitches. Cotton could not grow in the cold north, so every scrap was precious and passed down. For a long time, families were ashamed of boro as a sign of poverty. Now it is admired for its beauty and as a record of care and survival across generations.
artistBio: Boro was made by farming and fishing families, mostly women, over decades. The collector Chuzaburo Tanaka (1933–2013) spent his life gathering boro from Aomori, when few others valued it, and showed the world what it was. Boro has since shaped contemporary fashion and visible mending.

title: Baltimore Album Quilt
about: Each block of the quilt is different: baskets of flowers, wreaths, birds, ships, buildings and monuments of the city. Like a friendship album, blocks were often made and signed by different women and given together as a gift for a wedding, a departure or a minister. The quilts are a record of friendship, faith and local pride.
artistBio: Women in Baltimore's Methodist church communities made many of them. Some blocks are so refined that scholars believe a few skilled designers, possibly professionals, drew the patterns for others to sew. Their names often survive only as ink signatures on the cloth.

title: Bible Quilt
about: Eleven panels tell stories from the Bible: Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Jacob's ladder, the birth of Christ, the Crucifixion. The shapes are simple and strong, cut and sewn by hand and machine. Powers explained each scene in detail to the woman who bought it, so we know what she meant. The quilt is a sermon in cloth, from a woman who had been born enslaved.
artistBio: Harriet Powers (1837–1910) was born into slavery near Athens, Georgia. She showed this quilt at a cotton fair in 1886, and an artist named Jennie Smith later bought it from her during a hard time. A second quilt by Powers is at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. This one is at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

title: Hawaiian Quilt (Kapa Kuiki)
about: A single large design, cut from folded cloth like a paper snowflake, is sewn onto a plain background. Lines of quilting echo the shape outward like ripples on water. Patterns come from breadfruit, flowers and native plants. After the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy in 1893, women made flag quilts, called Kuʻu Hae Aloha, "my beloved flag," to keep the Hawaiian flag when it could no longer fly.
artistBio: Missionary women taught patchwork in the 1820s, but Hawaiian women turned it into something new. Patterns were treated as personal and sometimes kept secret. Quilting circles still pass designs and skills down today.

title: Quilts of Gee's Bend
artist: Mary Lee Bendolph, Annie Mae Young, Loretta Pettway and others
about: Bold, improvised quilts of strips and blocks, often made from worn work clothes. The women did not follow patterns. They built each quilt by eye, letting lines shift and colors clash. When the Whitney Museum showed them in 2002, critics compared them to modern abstract painting. For the makers, they were first of all warmth for their families and a way of keeping memory.
artistBio: Gee's Bend is a small, isolated Black community in Alabama, largely descended from people enslaved on the Pettway plantation. Women there quilted for generations. In 1966 some formed the Freedom Quilting Bee cooperative during the civil rights movement. Makers such as Mary Lee Bendolph and Loretta Pettway are now in major museums.

title: The AIDS Memorial Quilt
artist: Cleve Jones and thousands of makers
about: Each panel is three feet by six, about the size of a grave, and remembers one person who died of AIDS. Friends, partners and families made them with whatever they had: clothes, photos, sequins, letters. In 1987, when many people would not speak about the epidemic, the quilt was laid out on the National Mall. It now has around 50,000 panels and is one of the largest community art works in the world.
artistBio: Activist Cleve Jones came up with the idea in San Francisco in 1985 and helped found the NAMES Project. The first panels were made in 1987. Most makers were not artists at all, just people who were grieving. The quilt is now cared for by the National AIDS Memorial.

title: Six Prayers
medium: Cotton, linen, bast and silver thread
about: Six tall woven panels in quiet grays and whites, with threads that wander across them like lines of writing. The Jewish Museum in New York asked Albers to make a memorial to the six million Jews killed in the Holocaust. She avoided pictures of suffering and made something like a row of standing stones, or six columns of text no one can read. Silence is part of the meaning.
artistBio: Anni Albers (1899–1994) trained in the Bauhaus weaving workshop in Germany and left for the United States in 1933. She taught at Black Mountain College. In 1949 she became the first textile artist to have a solo exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art. Her book On Weaving (1965) is still read by weavers today.

title: We Are Living on a Star
about: A large tapestry of people and stars that hung in the government building in Oslo. Its title reflects her view that people share one fragile world. In 2011, a bomb attack on the government quarter damaged it badly. After careful conservation, it was shown again, carrying new meaning as a survivor of violence.
artistBio: Hannah Ryggen (1894–1970) was born in Sweden and lived on a farm on Norway's coast. She kept her own sheep, spun her own wool and dyed it with plants. She was self-taught and wove directly on the loom without drawings. Many of her tapestries protest war and fascism, including works on Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia and the Nazi occupation.

title: Abakans
about: Huge woven forms that hang from the ceiling, dark, folded and rough, some taller than a person. They pulled weaving off the wall and into the room as sculpture. Viewers have read them as wombs, wounds, cloaks or creatures. Abakanowicz said she wanted people to walk among them and feel them as living organisms.
artistBio: Magdalena Abakanowicz (1930–2017) grew up in Poland through the Second World War and worked under Communist rule. The Abakans, named after her, won a gold medal at the São Paulo Biennial in 1965. Later she made large crowds of headless figures from burlap and bronze. She changed how the art world saw fiber.

title: Tar Beach
medium: Acrylic on canvas with pieced fabric border
about: A painted story quilt. Eight-year-old Cassie Louise Lightfoot lies on her family's Harlem rooftop on a summer night and flies over the George Washington Bridge, which her father helped build. Text around the edges tells her story. Flying stands for freedom, and owning the bridge means claiming what her family built but was shut out of. Ringgold later turned it into a children's book.
artistBio: Faith Ringgold (1930–2024) was a painter, writer and activist from Harlem. She turned to quilts in the 1970s, partly inspired by her mother, a dressmaker, and by the long history of African American women's quilting. Tar Beach is at the Guggenheim Museum in New York.

title: Escalade Beyond Chromatic Lands
c: Sheila Hicks Escalade Beyond Chromatic Lands
about: A wall-high pile of soft, round bundles of color, pressed together like boulders or bales. Shown at the 2017 Venice Biennale, it invites the eye to climb, as the title says, from one color to the next. Hicks wants people to feel the weight and warmth of fiber and to see color as something with body.
artistBio: Sheila Hicks was born in Nebraska in 1934 and studied painting with Josef Albers at Yale. She traveled through South America studying Andean weaving, then settled in Paris. She works at every scale, from small woven studies she calls minimes to massive installations.

title: The Safety Patrol
medium: Quilted and appliquéd cotton, silk and velvet
about: A group of Black children in safety patrol belts, life-sized and full of color, built from layered fabric. Butler often starts from old black-and-white photographs and gives the people in them bright, patterned clothing and skin made of many fabrics. The children look straight at us, proud and serious. It is a portrait of dignity and childhood.
artistBio: Bisa Butler was born in 1973 in Orange, New Jersey, and trained as a painter at Howard University. Her grandmother sewed, and Butler turned to quilting as her main medium. A major solo show of her quilts opened at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2020.

title: Brain Forest Quipu
medium: Unspun wool, rope, found materials and sound
about: Huge white hanging forms of unspun wool, rope and found objects filled the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern. Vicuña drew on the Andean khipu, the knotted cord record, and asked what the cords might remember about forests being destroyed. Sound and song filled the space. She calls her work a way of mourning and also of listening.
artistBio: Cecilia Vicuña was born in Santiago, Chile, in 1948. She went into exile after the 1973 coup and has lived in London, Bogotá and New York. She is a poet as well as an artist. She received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2022.

title: The Lacemaker
about: A tiny painting, about the size of a sheet of paper, of a young woman bent over her bobbin lace. Everything leads to her hands and the fine threads. In the foreground, red and white threads spill from a cushion, painted loosely, almost like liquid. It is a picture of complete attention. Some viewers see in it the virtue of quiet domestic work; others see the joy of losing yourself in a task.
artistBio: Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) lived and worked in Delft. Only about 35 of his paintings survive. He painted slowly, mostly quiet rooms with one or two people in soft light. He was nearly forgotten after his death and rediscovered in the 19th century. The Lacemaker is at the Louvre in Paris.

title: Las Hilanderas (The Spinners)
about: In the front, women spin and wind wool in a dim workshop. In the bright alcove behind, ladies look at a tapestry while a helmeted figure raises her arm. This is the myth of Arachne, the weaver who challenged the goddess Athena to a contest and was turned into a spider. The painting places everyday work and myth side by side and asks what makes art: skill, inspiration or the gods.
artistBio: Diego Velázquez (1599–1660) was court painter to King Philip IV of Spain. He is best known for Las Meninas. This is one of his last works, painted with loose, rapid brushstrokes. It is in the Prado Museum in Madrid.

title: Weaver
about: A man sits nearly hidden inside the dark frame of a large wooden loom. The loom fills the picture, as it filled the weaver's small home and his whole day. Van Gogh admired the weavers' patience and hard lives. The painting is dark and heavy, and it treats manual work with seriousness and respect.
artistBio: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) lived with his parents in the village of Nuenen in 1883 to 1885. He made many paintings and drawings of local weavers there. This was before his move to Paris and the bright colors he is best known for. His weaver works are in the Van Gogh Museum and the Kröller-Müller Museum.

f: Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk.jpg
title: Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk
artist: Attributed to Emperor Huizong, after Zhang Xuan
medium: Ink and color on silk, handscroll
w: Court Ladies Preparing Newly Woven Silk
about: A handscroll that unrolls from right to left showing court women at work with newly woven silk. They pound it, sew it and stretch it out to iron it with a pan of hot coals. A girl ducks under the cloth to watch. It celebrates women's skill and the calm order of court life, and it reminds us that silk began as women's work.
artistBio: The scroll is a Song dynasty copy of a lost painting by Zhang Xuan, a Tang dynasty court painter of the 700s known for scenes of women. It is traditionally credited to Emperor Huizong (reigned 1100–1126), who was a painter and calligrapher himself, though it was likely done by artists of his painting academy. It is at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

title: The Tarkhan Dress
about: A linen shirt with a pleated top and narrow sleeves. It is the oldest woven garment known. It still has creases at the elbows and armpits, which suggests someone actually wore it. It is a plain piece of everyday clothing, and that is what makes it moving: a person five thousand years ago pulled this over their head.
artistBio: The maker is unknown, almost certainly someone in a household or workshop who spun flax and wove linen, which was ancient Egypt's main cloth. The archaeologist Flinders Petrie dug it up in 1913, but it sat unnoticed in a bundle of rags for decades. Radiocarbon dating in 2016 confirmed its age. It is at the Petrie Museum in London.

title: Plain Gauze Silk Robe
about: A full-length robe so fine it weighs less than 50 grams, lighter than a small bar of soap. It was buried with Xin Zhui, the Lady of Dai, along with many other silks. It shows how far Chinese silk technology had come more than two thousand years ago. It was clothing for the afterlife, meant to keep her life of comfort going after death.
artistBio: The weavers worked in Han dynasty workshops that raised silkworms, reeled the silk and wove it on complex looms, much of it women's work. Their names are not recorded. The tomb was excavated in the early 1970s and is one of the most important finds in China. The robe is in the Hunan Museum in Changsha.

title: Shōsōin Textiles
artist: Weavers of Tang China and Nara Japan
medium: Silk brocade, twill and dyed silk
about: In 756, after Emperor Shōmu died, his widow gave his treasures to the temple of Tōdai-ji, and they were sealed in a wooden storehouse. Among them are silks with hunting scenes, lions, and roundels in Persian style. These patterns traveled the Silk Road from Iran and Central Asia to China and then Japan. The storehouse is a time capsule of a connected world.
artistBio: Some of the silks were woven in Tang China and some in Japan, where weavers copied and adapted the imported designs. The makers are unknown. The Shōsōin is still cared for by the Imperial Household, and each autumn a small selection is shown at the Nara National Museum.

title: Wari Tapestry Tunic
about: At first glance it looks like a pattern of abstract stripes and blocks. Look longer, and you can find faces in profile, stretched and squeezed so much they almost disappear. They are figures linked to a staff-holding god. The tunics were worn by Wari leaders and show the power of a state that ruled much of the Andes before the Inca.
artistBio: Wari weavers produced some of the finest tapestry ever made, with a very high number of threads per inch. They most likely worked in state workshops, as Inca weavers did later. Their names are unknown. Wari tunics are in museums such as the Met in New York and Dumbarton Oaks.
f: Wari tunic - Textile Museum - Washington DC.jpg

title: The Shroud of Saint Josse
about: A silk with a row of elephants, camels and a border of walking camels, plus an inscription naming a Turkish commander in the Samanid state. It was made as a luxury cloth in the Islamic world. Later it reached France, probably with returning crusaders, and was used to wrap the relics of a Christian saint. One cloth carries two faiths and two worlds.
artistBio: It was woven in a court workshop in Khorasan, in today's Iran. The commander it names, Abu Mansur Bukhtegin, was executed in 961, which dates the silk. The weavers are unknown. It was kept for centuries at the abbey of Saint-Josse in northern France and is now in the Louvre.

title: The Cloth of Saint Gereon
about: Fragments of a large hanging with rows of roundels, each holding a griffin attacking a bull. The design copies costly silks from the Byzantine Empire, but it is woven in wool on a large scale. It is the oldest surviving European tapestry made as a wall hanging. It probably decorated the church of Saint Gereon in Cologne.
artistBio: The weavers are unknown and probably worked in or near Cologne. Their choice of design shows how much Western Europe admired Byzantine luxury goods. The fragments are now divided between museums in Lyon, Nuremberg and London.

title: The Baldishol Tapestry
about: A fragment showing two months of the year. April is a man standing under an arch. May is a knight on horseback. It was probably part of a longer calendar set showing all twelve months, a common theme in medieval churches. Simple, bold and full of color, it is one of the oldest tapestries in Europe.
artistBio: It was found in 1879 when the old Baldishol church was torn down. The weavers are unknown, likely local craftspeople working on an upright loom. It is in the National Museum in Oslo.
f: The Baldishol Tapestry - Baldisholteppet - OK-02862 - National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design.jpg

title: The Skog Tapestry
about: Small figures, horses and a church with bells. Three large figures on the left have been read as the Norse gods Odin, Thor and Freyr, or as three Christian kings. People are ringing the church bells, perhaps to drive away the old powers. Like the Överhogdal tapestries, it seems to show a time when old and new beliefs lived side by side.
artistBio: It was found in the church at Skog in northern Sweden. The makers are unknown, probably local women working in the farming community. It is now in the Swedish History Museum in Stockholm.

title: The Tapestry of Creation
about: Christ sits at the center of a great wheel, surrounded by the days of creation: light and dark, the waters, Adam naming the animals, Eve drawn from his side. Around the edge are the winds, the seasons and the months. It is the whole cosmos as people imagined it, with God at the center and human work set within the order of time.
artistBio: The makers are unknown. It was most likely made for Girona Cathedral, where it is still kept. The lower part is lost. Like the Bayeux Tapestry, it is embroidery rather than true tapestry.

title: Coronation Mantle of Roger II
about: A red silk half-circle cloak embroidered in gold. On each side a lion pounces on a camel, and a palm tree stands between them. An Arabic inscription along the edge wishes the wearer happiness and long life. It was made for a Christian Norman king by Muslim craftsmen, and later became the coronation robe of Holy Roman Emperors.
artistBio: It was made in the royal workshop in Palermo, where Arab, Greek and Norman cultures mixed under King Roger II. The inscription gives the year in the Islamic calendar. The craftsmen are not named. It is in the Imperial Treasury in Vienna.
f: Pluviale of the holy roman empire.jpg

title: The Quedlinburg Knotted Rug
about: A large knotted carpet showing the Marriage of Mercury and Philology, a Latin allegory of learning. Figures stand in rows like a procession. It is the oldest knotted carpet made in Europe that survives. It shows a convent of educated women stitching a story about the union of eloquence and learning.
artistBio: It was made by the nuns of Quedlinburg Abbey under Abbess Agnes II, a convent known for scholarship and fine work. Only fragments remain. They are kept in the treasury of the abbey church.

title: The Devonshire Hunting Tapestries
about: Four huge tapestries full of people hunting boar, bear, otter and swan, and flying falcons. Everyone is dressed in the latest courtly fashion: tall hats, long sleeves, rich fabrics. They are as much about showing off style as about hunting. They are a window into the clothes, manners and pastimes of a medieval court.
artistBio: They were woven in a major tapestry center of the time, probably Arras or Tournai. The designers and weavers are unknown. They belonged for centuries to the Dukes of Devonshire and are now at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: The Sistine Chapel Tapestries
medium: Wool, silk, gold and silver thread
about: Ten tapestries showing the lives of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, made to hang on the lower walls of the Sistine Chapel, under Michelangelo's ceiling. At the time, tapestries cost far more than paintings. They tell the story of the Church's founding, with the pope as heir to Peter.
artistBio: Pope Leo X commissioned them. Raphael painted full-size designs, called cartoons, and the weaving was done in Brussels in the workshop of Pieter van Aelst. Seven cartoons survive at the Victoria and Albert Museum. The tapestries are in the Vatican Museums.
f: Raphael, The Miraculous Draught of Fishes. Vatican Museums.jpg

title: The Oxburgh Hangings
artist: Mary, Queen of Scots and Bess of Hardwick
medium: Silk and wool embroidery on linen canvas
about: Dozens of small embroidered panels with plants, animals, sea creatures and emblems, many copied from natural history books. Some carry hidden messages. One shows a ginger cat playing with a mouse, often read as Queen Elizabeth toying with her captive cousin Mary. Needlework was something to pass the long days and a quiet way to speak.
artistBio: Mary, Queen of Scots, made them while she was a prisoner in England, together with Bess of Hardwick, the wife of her jailer, the Earl of Shrewsbury. The two women spent many hours stitching side by side. The hangings belong to the Victoria and Albert Museum and are shown at Oxburgh Hall in Norfolk.

title: Feather Headdress (Penacho)
medium: Quetzal and other feathers, gold, fiber netting
about: A great fan of long green quetzal feathers, layered with blue, red and brown feathers and small gold plates. It is often linked to the emperor Moctezuma, though that is not certain. For the Mexica, feathers were more precious than gold, and quetzal green meant life and fertility. It is one of very few such pieces to survive the conquest.
artistBio: It was made by the amanteca, specialist featherworkers who tied and glued feathers onto fiber netting and backing. They held a high place in Mexica society. The headdress reached Europe in the 1500s and is now in the Weltmuseum in Vienna. Mexico has asked for its return.

title: Ottoman Sultans' Kaftans
artist: Imperial workshops of Istanbul and Bursa
about: Long silk robes covered with huge tulips, carnations, and a pattern of three balls and wavy lines called çintamani. The Topkapı Palace kept the sultans' own robes after their deaths, often with labels, so many still survive. Kaftans were also given as robes of honor, a public sign of the sultan's favor.
artistBio: Designers in the palace workshop drew the patterns, and weavers in Bursa and Istanbul produced the silks. Both men and women worked in the silk trade. Most names are lost. The collection is in the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul.
f: Ottoman kaftan Inside of Topkapi palace Museum 5.jpg

title: Maya Huipil
about: The huipil is a loose blouse woven on a backstrap loom, one end tied to a tree and the other to the weaver's waist. The patterns and colors often tell which town a woman is from. Some designs hold old meanings about the cosmos, the sun's path and nature. Wearing a huipil is a statement of identity.
artistBio: Huipiles are woven by Maya women, who learn from their mothers and grandmothers. In Maya tradition, weaving was taught by the moon goddess Ixchel. A fine huipil can take months. Many weavers today work in cooperatives that protect their designs and income.

title: Saltillo Sarape
about: A long blanket worn as a cloak, with a large diamond at its center on a field of tiny, vibrating zigzags. The center has a slit or opening so it could be worn over the head. These sarapes were luxury items for wealthy horsemen. Their bold designs influenced Diné (Navajo) weavers to the north.
artistBio: The weavers worked on treadle looms in and around Saltillo, mixing Spanish loom technology with Indigenous tapestry skill. Many were Tlaxcalan settlers. Their names are not recorded.

title: Zapotec Rugs of Teotitlán
about: Wool rugs with stepped geometric frets based on the stone carvings of the nearby ancient city of Mitla. Many are dyed with cochineal, a red from tiny insects, indigo, and plants like marigold. The village has woven for centuries, and its rugs carry Zapotec identity into homes around the world.
artistBio: Weaving in Teotitlán is a family business, passed down through generations. Families raise or buy wool, card and spin it, dye it, and weave on treadle looms brought by the Spanish. Many weavers now sell directly from their homes and cooperatives.
f: Tapete de Lana de Teotitlan, Oaxaca.jpg

title: Tenango Embroidery
about: Bright animals, birds and plants embroidered on white cotton, often in a single color or a rainbow of threads. The creatures come from Otomí life and from old cave paintings in the area. Tenangos are playful and full of movement. They show a world where plants and animals are alive and connected.
artistBio: Otomí women in Tenango de Doria began making these embroideries in the 1960s, after a drought, as a way to earn money. They built on older Otomí embroidery. Often one person draws the design and another stitches it. Their work is widely copied by companies, and communities have fought to protect it.

title: Wixárika Yarn Painting (Nierika)
artist: Wixárika (Huichol) artists, including José Benítez Sánchez
medium: Yarn pressed into beeswax on wood
about: Images made by pressing colored yarn, strand by strand, into a board coated with beeswax. They show gods, animals, corn and the sacred pilgrimage to Wirikuta, the desert where the Wixárika believe the world was created. A nierika is a kind of window into the spirit world, and each image tells a story.
artistBio: The Wixárika people of western Mexico long made small yarn offerings. In the mid-1900s artists began making larger yarn paintings to sell. José Benítez Sánchez (1938–2009) was among the greatest, creating huge, complex works that are now in museums.

title: Shipibo-Konibo Kené Textiles
about: Mazes of fine lines in black, red or white, spreading over cloth like a living network. These designs, called kené, are tied to songs used in healing. Some say the patterns can be sung and the songs can be seen. Each piece is unique and comes from the maker's own vision.
artistBio: Kené is women's knowledge, passed from mother to daughter. Women paint designs with plant dyes or embroider them on cloth, and also paint pottery and faces. Peru declared kené part of its national cultural heritage in 2008.

title: Textiles of Taquile Island
artist: Quechua men and women of Taquile
about: On Taquile, clothing is a language. The patterns and colors of a man's knit cap show whether he is single or married and whether he holds a role in the community. Women weave belts with symbols of the farming year. The island's textile tradition was recognized by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible heritage.
artistBio: Unusually, men do the knitting on Taquile, starting as boys, while women spin and weave. The island's community also runs its own tourism, so visitors buy directly from makers. Their skills are passed down within families.

title: Ngatu (Tongan Tapa)
medium: Beaten bark of the paper mulberry, natural pigments
about: The inner bark of the paper mulberry tree is soaked and beaten into thin sheets, then joined into large cloths, sometimes many meters long. Designs in brown and black are rubbed on from carved boards or painted by hand. Tapa is given at weddings, funerals and royal occasions. A large ngatu stands for a family's wealth and care.
artistBio: In Tonga, women make ngatu together in groups, sharing the work of beating, joining and decorating. The rhythm of the beating mallets was once a sound of every village. Tapa traditions are found across the Pacific, from Fiji to Samoa to Hawaiʻi.

title: Māori Cloaks (Kākahu)
about: Cloaks made from muka, the silky fiber scraped from flax leaves, finger-woven without a loom. Some are covered in feathers, such as the kahu kiwi, made with kiwi feathers. Cloaks are treasures, or taonga, passed down through families. They are worn at important events and placed over the dead or over people being honored.
artistBio: Māori weavers, mostly women, learn from elders, and the work carries spiritual rules. Many traditions nearly disappeared in the 1900s, but master weavers such as Diggeress Te Kanawa (1920–2009) helped revive them. New cloaks are made today for graduations, ceremonies and family.

title: T'nalak
artist: T'boli dream weavers, including Lang Dulay
about: T'nalak is woven from abaca, a fiber from a relative of the banana plant. The threads are tied and dyed before weaving, in deep red, black and natural cream. The T'boli say the designs come to weavers in dreams, given by Fu Dalu, the spirit of the abaca. The cloth is used at births, weddings and deaths, and is treated as sacred.
artistBio: Lang Dulay (1928–2015) was a master T'boli weaver who knew more than a hundred designs. In 1998 the Philippines named her a National Living Treasure. She ran a weaving center to teach young women, so the dream patterns would not be lost.
f: T'nalak cloth of the T'boli people from Lake Sebu.jpg

title: Songket
medium: Silk or cotton with gold or silver thread
about: Songket is cloth with extra threads of gold or silver floated across the surface, making shining flowers, stars and geometric patterns. It was once worn only by royalty and nobles. Today it is still worn at weddings and important ceremonies. Its glitter is meant to show honor, beauty and celebration.
artistBio: Songket is mostly woven by women on traditional looms, in centers such as Palembang in Sumatra and Terengganu in Malaysia. A single piece can take weeks or months. The skills are passed down within families and weaving villages.

title: Ulos
about: Ulos are long woven cloths in deep reds, browns and blacks. They are given at the important moments of life: to a pregnant woman, a newborn, a married couple and the dead. The giving is a ceremony in itself. Draping an ulos over someone's shoulders is a way of giving them warmth, blessing and protection.
artistBio: Ulos are woven by Batak women on backstrap looms. Each type has its own name and use. Weaving was once part of every girl's upbringing, and today weaving groups work to keep the older patterns alive.

title: Sumba Hinggi
about: Large cloths worn by men, covered with horses, deer, roosters, lobsters and sometimes tall trees hung with skulls, a memory of old headhunting days. The colors come from indigo and a red root dye. Hinggi were signs of rank and were wrapped around the dead at funerals, in great numbers for nobles.
artistBio: Sumbanese women tie and dye the threads in many stages, a process that can take months, then weave them. Noble families once kept their own weavers and dyers. The craft continues in eastern Sumba, now also for collectors and visitors.
f: Man’s Shoulder Cloth (Hinggi), early 20th century; cotton; warp ikat; Indonesia, East Sumba, Kingdom of Kapunduk.jpg

title: Bojagi (Korean Wrapping Cloth)
medium: Patchwork of silk, ramie and cotton
about: Bojagi are cloths for wrapping and carrying things, from gifts to bedding. The patchwork kind, called jogakbo, was made by ordinary women from leftover scraps of clothing. The result looks like modern abstract painting, with blocks of color and fine seams. Wrapping something was believed to wrap in good fortune too.
artistBio: Bojagi were made at home by women whose names were never recorded. They were everyday objects, not thought of as art. The collector Huh Dong-hwa helped change that, gathering bojagi and showing them in his Museum of Korean Embroidery in Seoul.

title: Ainu Attus Robe
medium: Elm-bark fiber cloth with appliqué and embroidery
about: Robes woven from the inner bark of the elm tree, then decorated around the collar, cuffs and hem with bold swirls and spikes of appliqué and embroidery. The patterns guard the openings of the garment, where bad spirits might enter. The robe protects the body and also the person's spirit.
artistBio: Ainu women made attus, gathering and soaking bark, spinning it into thread and weaving on a backstrap loom. Each woman developed her own patterns, often passed to her daughters. After long pressure to give up Ainu culture, artists today are reviving these skills.

title: Bingata
about: Bright yellow, red and blue cloth with flowers, birds, waves and clouds. Patterns are made with paper stencils and a rice paste that resists the dye. Bingata was worn by the royal family and nobles of the Ryukyu Kingdom, and its strong colors fit Okinawa's light and sea.
artistBio: Bingata was made by families of dyers who served the court. Much was destroyed in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945. After the war, dyers such as Shiroma Eiki gathered surviving stencils and rebuilt the craft, sometimes using old records and found materials.

title: Edo-Period Kosode
about: The kosode is the ancestor of the kimono. Instead of a repeating pattern, the whole garment was treated as one picture: a sweep of waves, a bridge, falling maple leaves. Wealthy merchants spent fortunes on them, until laws in the 1680s banned the most costly gold embroidery. Designers responded with new techniques like yūzen dyeing.
artistBio: Kosode were made in workshops in Kyoto by teams of designers, dyers and embroiderers. Pattern books were sold so customers could choose designs. The painter Miyazaki Yūzensai is linked with the yūzen dyeing method that let artists paint detailed images on silk.
f: 白縮緬地橘文字模様小袖-Robe (Kosode) with Mandarin Orange Tree and Auspicious Characters MET 2002.325.jpg

title: Qing Dragon Robe
about: A court robe covered in dragons among clouds, with striped waves and mountains along the hem. The design is a map of the universe: earth, sea and sky, with the wearer at the center. Nine dragons were the rule, one hidden on the inside. Five-clawed dragons belonged to the emperor and his family.
artistBio: Dragon robes were made in imperial workshops in Nanjing, Suzhou and Hangzhou, where thousands of weavers and embroiderers worked. Designs were set by the court. Individual makers were not recorded.

title: Thongdrel
about: A thongdrel is a giant appliqué image of the Buddha or a saint, sometimes several stories tall. It is unrolled on a monastery wall at dawn on the last day of a festival and rolled up before the sun is high. The name means something like "liberation by seeing." People believe simply seeing it frees them from wrongdoing.
artistBio: Thongdrels are made by teams of trained artists, often monks, who cut and stitch hundreds of pieces of silk. A new one can take years. They are kept rolled up and shown only once a year.

title: Patola
about: In patola, both the lengthwise and crosswise threads are tied and dyed before weaving, and they must line up perfectly to form the pattern. Elephants, parrots, flowers and diamonds appear crisp on both sides. Patola were so prized that they were traded to Southeast Asia, where royal families treated them as sacred heirlooms.
artistBio: Only a few families still make true double-ikat patola, most famously the Salvi family of Patan. A single sari can take months of work by several people. The skill has been passed down within the family for centuries.

title: Palampore (Painted Chintz)
about: A large bedcover with a flowering tree rising from a little hill, its branches full of exotic blossoms and birds. The colors are fast because they were made with mordants, chemical aids that fix dyes to cotton. Europeans went wild for this "chintz," so much that France banned imports for decades to protect its own industry.
artistBio: Indian artisans drew the designs with a bamboo pen, called a kalam, which gives the related craft kalamkari its name. Making one involved many stages of drawing, waxing, dyeing and washing. The makers adapted their designs to European taste. Their names were not recorded.

title: Chamba Rumal
artist: Women of Chamba with Pahari painters
about: Square cloths embroidered with scenes of Krishna and the cowherd girls, wedding processions and hunting. The stitch is the same on both sides, so there is no back. The designs were drawn by court painters, so a rumal looks like a miniature painting in thread. They were used to cover gifts at weddings and other exchanges.
artistBio: Women of the royal and noble households did the embroidery, often from outlines drawn by painters of the Pahari school. The tradition faded in the 20th century, but artisans in Chamba have since revived it.

title: Rabari Embroidery
about: Dense chain stitch in red, black and bright colors, studded with small round mirrors that catch the light. The patterns include scorpions, parrots, camels and temple forms. Embroidery was part of a bride's dowry and showed her skill and family pride. The mirrors were said to deflect the evil eye.
artistBio: The Rabari are herders who travel with camels, sheep and goats. Girls once spent years embroidering their dowry. In 1995, Rabari elders banned embroidered dowries to ease the burden on families, and women turned to quicker trims and to embroidery for sale.
f: Shawl from India, Rabari culture, Honolulu Museum of Art 6794.1.JPG

title: Ralli Quilts
artist: Women of Sindh and neighboring regions
about: Bright quilts of squares, triangles and cut-out shapes in red, yellow, white and black, held with neat rows of running stitch. They are used as bedding, seating and gifts. They are often made for a daughter's dowry. A ralli brings color and comfort to homes in a hot, dry land.
artistBio: Rallis are made by women of many communities, Muslim and Hindu, often working together in groups. Each region has its own style. Old saris and clothes are reused for the layers.

title: Turkmen Carpets
about: Deep red carpets covered with rows of medallions called guls. Each tribe, such as the Tekke, Yomut or Salor, had its own gul, so a carpet could show who made it. Nomadic families also wove bags to hang inside their tents for storage. The carpet is so central to Turkmen identity that it appears on the national flag.
artistBio: Turkmen carpets were woven by women on horizontal looms inside their tents. Girls learned young, and a large carpet was a major family treasure. Turkmenistan celebrates a national Carpet Day each spring.

title: Beni Ourain Rugs
artist: Amazigh (Berber) women of the Middle Atlas
about: Thick, soft rugs of natural cream wool with loose lines of dark brown or black forming diamonds. In the cold Atlas Mountains they were used as blankets and bedding. The designs are said to hold signs of protection and fertility. In the 20th century, modernist designers in Europe admired their simplicity.
artistBio: The rugs are woven by Amazigh women of the Beni Ourain tribes, using wool from their own sheep. Each weaver works freely, without a drawn pattern. Today many weavers sell through cooperatives.

title: Palestinian Tatreez
medium: Cross-stitch embroidery on cotton and linen
about: Tatreez is cross-stitch, worked in deep reds and other colors on the chest panels and sides of a woman's dress, the thobe. Different towns and villages had their own patterns, so a dress could show where a woman came from. Tatreez carries memory of places and families. UNESCO recognized it as intangible heritage in 2021.
artistBio: Women learned tatreez from mothers and grandmothers and stitched dresses for themselves and their daughters. Today, women in many countries keep the practice going in workshops and collectives, and designers use it in new ways.

title: Khayamiya (Tentmakers' Appliqué)
about: Hand-stitched panels of geometric stars, lotus flowers and arabesques in bright cotton on canvas. They line the tents used for weddings, funerals and festivals, turning plain spaces into colorful rooms. Many patterns echo the domes and tiles of Islamic architecture. Each piece is stitched entirely by hand.
artistBio: The craft is practiced mostly by men in the Street of the Tentmakers, a covered market in old Cairo near the Bab Zuwayla gate. Skills pass from father to son. Printed fabric has replaced much handwork for tents, and the remaining artisans now also make pieces for collectors.

title: Adire
about: Deep blue cloth with pale patterns. Some are tied or stitched before dyeing; others are painted with a starch paste using a feather or stencil. Patterns have names and meanings, from everyday objects to proverbs. Adire is a Yoruba art of patience, since the cloth is dipped in indigo again and again to deepen the blue.
artistBio: Adire has long been women's work, centered in cities such as Abeokuta and Ibadan. Women ran the dye pots and the trade. In recent decades, artists such as Nike Davies-Okundaye have trained new generations and brought adire to international audiences.

title: Fon Royal Appliqué
about: Colored cloth shapes stitched onto a dark background: a buffalo, a lion, a shark, a pineapple. Each image stands for a king of Dahomey and a saying linked to his reign. The hangings told the kingdom's history in pictures and decorated royal ceremonies. They worked like heraldry and history book in one.
artistBio: Appliqué makers in Abomey worked for the kings, organized in family guilds such as the Yemadje family. After the kingdom's fall, the guilds continued to make hangings, now for tourists and collectors as well.

title: Asafo Flags
about: Bright flags with bold images: a lion, a crocodile, a man with a cannon. Each one illustrates a proverb that boasts of the company's strength or teases its rivals. Asafo companies were traditional military and civic groups. Under British rule, many flags included a small Union Jack in the corner, later replaced by Ghana's flag.
artistBio: Flags were made by specialist male tailors and flag makers for each company. New flags are made for ceremonies and the installation of leaders. Older flags are now found in museum collections.

title: Lamba Akotifahana
about: Lamba are cloths worn wrapped around the body. The finest, akotifahana, have small patterns floating on the surface: flowers, birds and geometric shapes. Another kind of lamba, of wild silk, wraps the dead. In the famadihana ceremony, families rewrap the bones of ancestors in fresh lamba, keeping a close bond across generations.
artistBio: Merina women in the highlands around Antananarivo wove the finest lamba, once for royalty. The craft declined in the 20th century but has been revived by weavers such as the cooperative workshops around the capital.
f: Lamba raw silk shawl from Madagascar.jpg

title: Ribbon Work
artist: Great Lakes and Prairie Native women
place: Great Lakes and Prairies, North America
about: Strips of silk ribbon cut and layered into sharp, mirror-image designs, then sewn onto skirts, leggings and shawls. The ribbons first came from French traders, but the art form is entirely Native. Designs are often handed down in families. Ribbon work is worn proudly today at powwows and ceremonies.
artistBio: Women of many nations, including the Anishinaabe, Meskwaki and Osage, developed ribbon work. Each nation and family has its own style. Contemporary artists continue the tradition and use it in new forms of fashion and art.

title: Lakota Quillwork
about: Porcupine quills are softened, flattened between the teeth, dyed and then folded, wrapped or stitched onto hide. They make shining bands of color on shirts, moccasins and cradleboards. Quillwork is older than glass beadwork on the Plains. It carried spiritual meaning, and skilled quillworkers were highly respected.
artistBio: Lakota women did quillwork, sometimes as members of quillworkers' societies that honored excellence. When trade beads arrived, many turned to beadwork, but quillwork never disappeared. Artists today keep both traditions alive.

title: Pomo Feathered Baskets
medium: Sedge, willow, bulrush, feathers and shell
about: Small round baskets covered entirely in feathers: red from woodpeckers, green from mallard ducks, black topknots from quail, with shell beads hanging from the rim. Some are tiny. They were given as treasured gifts and sometimes burned or buried with the dead. Pomo baskets are among the finest ever made.
artistBio: Pomo women have woven baskets for generations, gathering and preparing their own plants. Mabel McKay (1907–1993) was a renowned weaver and healer who said her designs came to her in dreams. Her baskets are in the Smithsonian and other museums.

title: Degikup Baskets
medium: Willow, bracken fern root and redbud
about: Round, bowl-shaped baskets with tiny, even stitches and flame-like patterns climbing the sides. The degikup shape was her own development of Washoe tradition. Her work set a new standard for basketry as fine art. Its precision is astonishing, with dozens of stitches to the inch.
artistBio: Dat So La Lee was a Washoe weaver who died in 1925. Her work was sold through Abe and Amy Cohn, store owners in Carson City who promoted her and made up romantic stories about her baskets. Today her baskets are among the most valued in American art, and Washoe people tell her story in their own words.

title: Coast Salish Blankets
artist: Coast Salish weavers, including Debra Sparrow
place: Salish Sea region, British Columbia and Washington
about: Blankets of white wool with bold geometric patterns in black, red and yellow. They were made from mountain goat wool and from the fleece of a now-extinct breed of small woolly dog that Coast Salish people raised for its hair. Blankets were signs of wealth and were given away at potlatches and worn at ceremonies.
artistBio: Coast Salish women wove on upright looms. The tradition was nearly broken under colonial rule. In the 1980s, Musqueam weavers such as Debra Sparrow and her sisters relearned it by studying museum pieces, and they have since taught many others.

title: Baker Lake Wall Hangings
artist: Inuit women of Qamani'tuaq, including Jessie Oonark
medium: Wool duffel and felt appliqué and embroidery
about: Large hangings with strong shapes of people, animals, spirits and tools, cut from wool cloth and stitched onto a colored background. They show Inuit life on the land, stories and shamanic beings. The bold, flat shapes come from the women's long experience cutting and sewing caribou-skin clothing.
artistBio: Jessie Oonark (1906–1985) moved to Baker Lake after years of hardship on the land and became one of the most important Inuit artists. She drew and sewed, and her children became artists too. She was named an Officer of the Order of Canada in 1984.

title: Seminole Patchwork
about: Bands of tiny bright patterns made by sewing strips of cloth together, cutting them crosswise and sewing them again at angles. The bands are stacked into skirts and jackets full of color. Patterns have names, such as rain, fire and lightning. It is a distinctly Seminole art that grew out of new tools.
artistBio: Seminole women developed the technique in the early 1900s after hand-cranked sewing machines reached their camps in the Everglades. Women still make patchwork clothing for their families and for sale.

title: Amish Quilts
medium: Pieced and quilted wool and cotton
about: Large plain fields of deep purple, blue, red and green, built into simple shapes such as a central diamond or a field of small squares. Printed fabric was avoided, in keeping with the community's simple dress. Within the bold shapes, the quilting stitches are tiny and elaborate. When shown in art museums, they were compared to modern abstract painting.
artistBio: Amish women made quilts at home and at quilting bees, often from leftover dress fabric. Quilts were made for daily use and for weddings. Their names are seldom recorded, but quilts were treasured within families.

title: Grenfell Hooked Mats
artist: Women of Labrador and northern Newfoundland
medium: Hooked silk and rayon stockings on burlap
about: Small rugs showing dog teams, polar bears, icebergs, puffins and fishing boats, hooked from strips of dyed stockings. They capture the cold beauty of the northern coast. The mats were sold to visitors and through shops abroad, bringing cash into isolated fishing families.
artistBio: The Grenfell Mission, founded by the doctor Wilfred Grenfell, organized local women to make mats for sale. Donated silk stockings from the United States and Canada were used as material. The mat makers were paid for their work, and their names were sometimes stitched or written on labels.

title: Tjanpi Desert Weavers
artist: Women of the Central and Western Desert
medium: Native grasses, wool, raffia and found materials
about: Baskets and sculptures of animals, birds, people and even cars, made from bundled desert grass bound with colored wool. In 2005 the group won a major Aboriginal art prize with a life-size grass sculpture of a Toyota four-wheel drive, the vehicle that carries families across desert country. The work is humorous, warm and rooted in land.
artistBio: Tjanpi Desert Weavers is a social enterprise run by the women's council of the Ngaanyatjarra, Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara lands. Several hundred women from remote communities make work together, often while on country, and share stories as they weave.

title: Fair Isle Knitting
artist: Knitters of Fair Isle and Shetland
about: Rows of small, repeating patterns, crosses, stars and diamonds, knitted with two colors at a time in soft wool. The colors shift row by row in bands. Sweaters, hats and gloves made this way are warm and light. Fair Isle became a fashion when the Prince of Wales wore a sweater on the golf course in the 1920s.
artistBio: The knitters were mostly women on Fair Isle, a tiny island between Orkney and Shetland, and across Shetland. Knitting was a vital source of income for crofting families. Patterns were passed by eye and memory rather than written down.

title: Shetland Lace Shawl
about: Shawls knitted from wool spun so fine that a large shawl could be drawn through a wedding ring, which gave them the name "wedding ring shawls." The patterns have names like cat's paw, fern and horseshoe. They were treasured as christening shawls and gifts. Queen Victoria owned and admired them.
artistBio: Shetland women, especially on the island of Unst, spun the fine wool from local sheep and knitted the shawls. It was skilled, poorly paid work that helped families survive. The Shetland Museum and knitters today keep the patterns and skills alive.

title: Venetian Gros Point Lace
about: Needle lace with raised, curling flowers and scrolls, almost like carved ivory, worn as collars and cuffs by the rich and powerful. It took enormous time and skill. Lace was such a status symbol that Louis XIV's minister Colbert set up a French lace industry in 1665 to stop money flowing to Venice.
artistBio: Lace was made by women, often in convents and workshops, with a needle and a single thread, building the design stitch by stitch. Venice's lace industry declined in the 1700s, but a school on the island of Burano revived it in the 1870s.

title: Vyshyvanka
about: A shirt or blouse embroidered at the collar, chest and sleeves, often in red and black. Each region has its own patterns and colors. The designs were believed to protect the wearer, and a shirt might be passed down through generations. Today the vyshyvanka is a strong symbol of Ukrainian identity, celebrated on Vyshyvanka Day each May.
artistBio: Embroidery was traditionally done by women at home, with patterns learned from their mothers and grandmothers. Today, designers and community groups at home and abroad keep the tradition going and adapt it for new clothing.

title: Romanian Ie Blouse
about: A loose white blouse with embroidery on the sleeves, especially a band at the shoulder called the altiță. Patterns and colors once showed a woman's village, age and marital status. The blouse inspired painters and designers, including Matisse. UNESCO added the art of the ie to its intangible heritage list in 2022.
artistBio: Women embroidered ie at home, often for festivals and weddings, using patterns passed down in their families. Many villages had their own styles. Today, groups such as the community La Blouse Roumaine work to keep handmade ie alive.

title: Tartan
about: Colored stripes crossing at right angles make the familiar plaid. After the Jacobite rising of 1745, a 1746 law banned Highland dress, including tartan, for most men, and it was not lifted until 1782. Clan tartans as we know them were largely a 19th-century idea. Today, tartan is a symbol of Scottish identity worldwide.
artistBio: Tartan was woven by local weavers in the Highlands using local dyes. Later, mills such as Wilsons of Bannockburn standardized patterns and named them. New tartans are still designed and registered today.

title: Strawberry Thief
about: Thrushes steal strawberries among flowers and leaves on a deep blue ground. Morris was inspired by birds raiding the fruit at his country home, Kelmscott Manor. The design was printed by hand with wooden blocks, a slow process he chose over machine printing. It is one of the most loved patterns of the Arts and Crafts movement.
artistBio: William Morris (1834–1896) was a designer, writer and socialist who believed in beautiful, handmade things for daily life. He revived natural dyeing and block printing at his works at Merton Abbey. Strawberry Thief became one of his most popular designs.

title: The Holy Grail Tapestries
about: A series telling the story of the knights of King Arthur searching for the Holy Grail. Pale, still figures move through flowering forests. Only Galahad, the pure knight, reaches the vision of the Grail. The tapestries combine medieval legend, Christian longing and the Arts and Crafts love of handwork.
artistBio: Edward Burne-Jones designed the figures, while Morris and his assistant John Henry Dearle designed the backgrounds and plants. They were woven at Morris & Co.'s Merton Abbey works for Stanmore Hall. One set is at Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.

title: 5 Chöre (Five Choirs)
medium: Jacquard-woven cotton, wool, rayon and silk
about: A wall hanging of shifting bands and grids of color, like music turned into woven form. The title suggests five voices singing together. Stölzl made the loom work like a painter's canvas but kept the logic of threads and structure. It is a key work of modern weaving.
artistBio: Gunta Stölzl (1897–1983) was the first woman to become a master at the Bauhaus, where she led the weaving workshop. She was forced out in 1931, partly because of her marriage to a Jewish architect. She moved to Zurich and ran a hand-weaving business for the rest of her career.

title: Crib Blanket for Her Son
about: A small blanket of rectangles and triangles in bright colors, sewn for her baby son. She based it on peasant blankets she remembered from her childhood in Ukraine. Looking at it later, she and her husband saw a new way of thinking about color. It helped spark their abstract art.
artistBio: Sonia Delaunay (1885–1979) was born in Ukraine and became a leading abstract painter and designer in Paris. She moved freely between painting, fashion, textiles and theater design. The blanket is at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

title: Christ in Glory in the Tetramorph
w: Christ in Glory in the Tetramorph
about: One of the largest tapestries in the world, behind the altar of the new Coventry Cathedral, built after the old one was bombed in 1940. Christ sits enthroned, surrounded by the four symbols of the Gospel writers. A small human figure stands between his feet, showing how small and how protected a person is before God.
artistBio: Graham Sutherland (1903–1980) was a British painter. He worked on the design for about ten years. The tapestry was woven by the Pinton workshop in Felletin, France, on a huge loom, with a team of weavers.

title: Le Chant du Monde
about: Ten huge tapestries on black backgrounds. The early ones show the threat of the atomic bomb and the horror of Hiroshima. The later ones celebrate water, fire, poetry and the conquest of space. Lurçat made them after seeing the medieval Apocalypse Tapestry in Angers. They are a modern Apocalypse that ends in hope.
artistBio: Jean Lurçat (1892–1966) was a French painter who led the revival of tapestry in the 20th century. He developed a simple system of numbered colors so weavers could follow his designs. The series hangs in a former medieval hospital in Angers.

title: Golden Woven Works
medium: Linen, cotton, gesso, gold and silver leaf
about: Woven surfaces covered in gesso and gold leaf that shimmer like walls of a church or the treasures of ancient Colombia. Some hang in long strands like rain or mist. They are about light, landscape and the sacred. Amaral calls them a way of understanding time and memory.
artistBio: Olga de Amaral was born in Bogotá in 1932. She studied at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Michigan and returned to Colombia to work. She drew on pre-Columbian gold work and colonial church gilding. In 2024 the Fondation Cartier in Paris held a major retrospective of her work.

title: Woven Forms
about: Tall, narrow hangings with open spaces where the warp threads show, some flaring out at the bottom like wings or flames. Tawney freed weaving from the flat rectangle. Her later "Cloud" works were made of thousands of hanging threads. Many of her pieces have a quiet, meditative feeling.
